title: RHCE Enterprise Linux
description: Prepare for EX342 after RHCSA. Diagnose and restore AlmaLinux 10 hosts through controlled incidents covering boot, encrypted storage, RPM, networking, applications, PAM and crash evidence. Includes independent practicals and a two-host final.

modules.title: Recover files, volumes and encrypted data
Debug application failures without relaxing controls
Diagnose identity, admission and account policy

lessons.title: Build a record another shift can reproduce
topics: Build a record another shift can reproduce
lessons.body:
At 09:10 one request took ten seconds. That establishes an observation, but neither the affected machine nor the cause. Start with a test that names the client, server, operation, expected result and actual time. Preserve one healthy control. A selective repair is possible only after learning where the paths diverge.

Use two disposable AlmaLinux 10 guests named **station** and **relay**, reachable on an isolated private network. Station runs the service. Relay provides a second viewpoint and later receives logs. Use RHCSA-level shell, editor, systemd, networking and storage skills. Take offline snapshots of both guests before changing them. Read **Lab setup and reset** in References for packages and addresses. The EX342 exam page names RHEL 10.2. Record the actual AlmaLinux build so differences in package versions remain visible.

```console
> hostnamectl --static
station (relay on the other guest)
> cat /etc/os-release
The release file includes ID="almalinux" and VERSION_ID for the installed 10.x build.
> cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
A UUID identifying this boot; retain the value for the later comparison.
> date -u +%FT%TZ
One UTC timestamp, for example 2026-11-24T09:10:00Z.
> uptime
Current time, uptime, user count and load averages for 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
> free -h
Mem: and Swap: rows with human-readable capacities; record available memory.
> vmstat 1 5
Five data rows. The first normally summarizes activity since boot; the next four sample one-second intervals.
> df -hT /
One row for the filesystem serving /, with filesystem type, size, available space and use percentage.
> df -i /
The same mount with inode totals, used and free counts and inode-use percentage.
```

The first vmstat row normally summarizes activity since boot. Use the later intervals to investigate a live stall. A nearly full block count and exhausted inode count can cause the same write error through different mechanisms. A high load average includes runnable work and tasks in uninterruptible sleep. Compare CPU idle time, runnable tasks and blocked tasks before calling it CPU contention.

On station find the manual sections for vmstat and journalctl with `man -k vmstat` and `man journalctl`. Record one field definition and reproduce it during a short, bounded workload. In Cockpit open the Overview and metrics/history views available in your build. Compare the same machine, UTC interval and memory measure with the shell record. Historical charts require a configured collector such as PCP. A blank graph is missing evidence. Record the socket/service and collector state before changing either.

On station with man pages installed.

```console
> man -k vmstat
Name/section and one-line descriptions from the local manual index; local index contents can vary.
> man journalctl
The journalctl manual opens in the configured pager. Press q to return.
```

lessons.title: Follow one message from producer to collector
topics: Follow one message from producer to collector
lessons.body:
A sender can accept a local log message while a central dashboard remains silent. Break the path into local acceptance, sender action, network delivery, receiver input and receiver storage. Give the test an unpredictable marker. Finding last week's message proves nothing about this run.

In this private exercise assume relay has address 192.0.2.22 and station has 192.0.2.21. Use the actual private addresses from setup. On relay place the following in a new root-owned `/etc/rsyslog.d/30-erudior-receiver.conf`. Check that imtcp has not already been loaded elsewhere. Add the receiver rule only once.

```text
module(load="imtcp")
ruleset(name="erudiorRemote") {
  if $programname == "desk-case" then /var/log/erudior-remote.log
}
input(type="imtcp" port="514" ruleset="erudiorRemote")
```

On station put the following sender action in a dedicated rsyslog drop-in. Replace the example destination before use.

```text
if $programname == "desk-case" then action(type="omfwd" target="192.0.2.22" port="514" protocol="tcp" queue.type="linkedList")
```

Run `sudo rsyslogd -N1` on each guest. Restart rsyslog only where validation succeeds. On relay allow 514/tcp only on the private lab network using its assigned firewalld zone or a rich rule limited to station's address. Verify the listener with `ss -lnt`. On station use `marker="case-$(date +%s)-$$"` and `logger -t desk-case "$marker"`. Find that exact marker in station's journal and relay's dedicated log. Record both timestamps. This demo uses TCP on an isolated network. Outside the exercise, authenticate endpoints and encrypt transport under site policy.

Validate on each guest before restarting rsyslog.

```console
> sudo rsyslogd -N1
Validation diagnostics end with End of config validation run when successful. Fix errors before restart.
```

Relay, after activating the validated receiver.

```console
> ss -lnt
A LISTEN row includes the receiver address and TCP port 514.
```

Station, same shell for both commands. Check this marker on both machines.

```console
> marker="case-$(date +%s)-$$"
No output; marker contains this run’s timestamp and shell PID.
> logger -t desk-case "$marker"
No output on successful submission to local logging. Remote delivery requires a separate check.
```

Stop the receiver service briefly and submit another marker. Restore the receiver and compare observed delivery and sender diagnostics. Repeated or absent messages are possible under outages and restarts, and an in-memory queue is transient. Report what you actually observed and whether the application that produced the message continued working.

lessons.title: Separate approved changes from unexplained drift
topics: Separate approved changes from unexplained drift
lessons.body:
Ansible expresses the state you intend to deploy. AIDE compares observed attributes against a previously trusted baseline. They answer different questions. A repair run can erase the evidence needed to explain an alert, so capture the comparison before repairing anything.

On station, create the directory for the marker.

```console
> sudo install -d -m 0755 /srv/erudior-check
No output on success. The exercise directory exists with mode 0755.
```

On relay, prepare a one-host inventory using the verified SSH identity from setup. Save this play as `marker.yml`.

```yaml
- name: Declare the desk marker
  hosts: station
  become: true
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: Publish the approved marker
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: /srv/erudior-check/owner
        content: "desk=blue\n"
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: '0644'
```

On relay, preview the change, apply it and repeat to establish an idempotent baseline. Supply the become password if your administrator account requires it.

```console
> ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini marker.yml --limit station --check --diff
On a fresh target Ansible predicts a changed copy task and shows the proposed content. The target stays unchanged.
> ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini marker.yml --limit station
On a fresh target the copy task reports changed and creates the owner file.
> ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini marker.yml --limit station
With the same inputs, the recap for station includes changed=0 and failed=0.
```

On station use a separate AIDE configuration for the lab and avoid replacing the system baseline. As root create `/root/desk-aide.conf` containing these four lines. AIDE regex rules select the exercise directory and its contents. Use explicit local database paths and an uncompressed output for this small exercise.

```text
database_in=file:/root/desk-aide.db
database_out=file:/root/desk-aide.new
gzip_dbout=no
/srv/erudior-check p+u+g+s+sha256
```

In a root shell on station, initialize the separate lab database. Review the initialization report and confirm its success before installing the baseline.

```console
> aide -c /root/desk-aide.conf --init
AIDE reports initialization and writes /root/desk-aide.new. Inspect and install the reviewed baseline at the configured input path before checking.
```

```console
> install -m 0600 /root/desk-aide.new /root/desk-aide.db
No output on success. The reviewed baseline is installed with owner-only access.
> aide -c /root/desk-aide.conf --check
AIDE reports that no differences were found and returns status 0.
> chmod 0600 /srv/erudior-check/owner
No output on success. The marker now has different permissions.
> aide -c /root/desk-aide.conf --check
AIDE lists /srv/erudior-check/owner with a changed permissions attribute and returns a nonzero difference status. Retain this report.
```

On relay, restore the declared permissions, then repeat the same play.

```console
> ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini marker.yml --limit station
The copy task reports changed and restores the mode to 0644.
> ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini marker.yml --limit station
The recap for station includes changed=0 and failed=0.
```

In the root shell on station, compare against the original protected database. Rebuilding the database after the change would accept the incorrect mode.

```console
> aide -c /root/desk-aide.conf --check
No differences are reported and the check returns status 0.
```

## Independent practical

The night shift suspects a drifted mode in /srv/erudior-check/owner on station. Relay needs a unique case marker and a short report of current load. Use the guided configuration with a fresh baseline, then have a partner alter the file mode. For a solo run set mode 0600 after saving a clean baseline and before starting the case. Preserve station and relay access throughout.

```assignment
lab: cases-practical
```

lessons.title: Read the failed dependency before changing the service
topics: Read the failed dependency before changing the service
lessons.body:
A VM reaches its login prompt, but the morning desk report never appears. The kernel and login service clearly started. Separate a unit failing in a healthy boot from a filesystem or initramfs problem that prevents the operating system from reaching that point.

On station save this file as `/etc/systemd/system/erudior-dispatch.service`. Use a clean lab snapshot. The deliberate missing file is confined to the exercise.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Erudior desk receipt
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/test -r /etc/erudior-desk/ready
RemainAfterExit=yes
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, enable the unit and start it. Inspect `systemctl status erudior-dispatch.service`, `journalctl -b -u erudior-dispatch.service`, and `systemctl cat erudior-dispatch.service`. The process itself exits with a failure status because its input is missing. A successful syntax check cannot establish a readable input. A spec under `WantedBy` allows unrelated targets to complete even when the service fails.

Station, after saving the unit; the readiness file is initially missing.

```console
> sudo systemctl daemon-reload
No output on success. systemd rereads the unit definitions.
> sudo systemctl enable erudior-dispatch.service
A new enablement normally reports the created symlink under multi-user.target.wants.
> sudo systemctl start erudior-dispatch.service
The start fails because /usr/bin/test cannot read the missing input.
> systemctl status erudior-dispatch.service
Active: failed, with the ExecStart test exiting with status 1.
> journalctl -b -u erudior-dispatch.service
This boot’s entries show the attempted start and the unit failure.
> systemctl cat erudior-dispatch.service
The effective unit source and any drop-ins include ExecStart=/usr/bin/test -r /etc/erudior-desk/ready.
```

On station, locate the first missing path component.

```console
> namei -l /etc/erudior-desk/ready
Components are listed with modes and owners until the first missing component.
```

On this fresh snapshot, create the dedicated directory and the root-owned, mode-0644 marker. Start the unit again and read the file independently.

```console
> sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/erudior-desk
No output on success. The dedicated directory exists.
> printf 'desk-ready\n' | sudo tee /etc/erudior-desk/ready >/dev/null
No terminal output. The marker contains desk-ready followed by a newline.
> sudo chmod 0644 /etc/erudior-desk/ready
No output on success. The new root-owned file is readable by the service.
> sudo systemctl start erudior-dispatch.service
No output on success.
> systemctl is-active erudior-dispatch.service
active
> cat /etc/erudior-desk/ready
desk-ready
```

The oneshot unit should be active (exited) because it retains active status. Reboot the snapshot clone and capture a new boot ID, status and receipt before changing anything else. Compare with a second trial where a drop-in overrides the input path. Reading the base unit alone misses that fault.

lessons.title: Choose a recovery boundary at the console
topics: Choose a recovery boundary at the console
lessons.body:
Draw the sequence for your guest: firmware chooses a disk; its boot loader selects a kernel and initramfs; the initramfs locates the root volume; systemd in the installed operating system mounts remaining filesystems and starts the target. Where did output stop? A root device that never appeared and a failed required non-root mount may both show an emergency prompt but require different evidence.

Practice first without breaking boot. In the console compare `cat /proc/cmdline`, `findmnt /`, `lsblk -f`, `systemctl --failed` and `journalctl --list-boots`. A previous boot appears only if its journal survived. On a snapshot clone, an instructor adds an invalid UUID entry for a **lab-only** mount to a separate working copy of fstab. Run `findmnt --verify --verbose --tab-file ./fstab.trial`. Compare the failure with actual UUIDs. Make exactly one correction in that working copy. Unverified fstab experiments on the root volume are outside this exercise.

Normal guest console; examine one boot before staging faults.

```console
> cat /proc/cmdline
The running kernel arguments as one line. Parameters depend on this guest.
> findmnt /
A row for / with its source, filesystem type and mount options.
> lsblk -f
Device hierarchy, filesystem types, UUIDs and mountpoints.
> systemctl --failed
Failed units are listed; a healthy guest can report 0 loaded units listed.
> journalctl --list-boots
Boot indices, boot IDs and time ranges. Older boots appear only if retained.
```

Snapshot clone; check the working copy only.

```console
> findmnt --verify --verbose --tab-file ./fstab.trial
A diagnostic identifies the unresolved lab source. Read all reported problems and warnings.
```

For a console recovery rehearsal, keep a snapshot and trusted installation media. Boot the clone into the installer's rescue environment and identify which system is mounted and where. On RHEL-family rescue media the installed root is commonly under `/mnt/sysroot`; the rescue screen is authoritative. Inspect the installed fstab and saved journal read-only first. Distinguish the rescue environment's root from the installed root by checking release files and mount identities. Use the authorized console recovery procedure in the media documentation when a repair requires write access. Remove the media and boot the installed system to verify the result.

Now stage an actual non-root mount fault on an **offline-snapshotted clone**. This exercise boots the normal OS and leaves the console available. As root choose a new lab-only filename and unused mountpoint. Create a 64 MiB file at /var/tmp/erudior-boot.ext4 with truncate, make an ext4 filesystem inside that regular file, and create /mnt/erudior-boot. Save the original fstab and add only the following row with the deliberately wrong backing filename:

```text
/var/tmp/erudior-missing.ext4 /mnt/erudior-boot ext4 loop,nofail 0 0
```

Reboot the clone. The optional mount fails while the normal target remains available. At the authorized console use journalctl -b, findmnt --mountpoint /mnt/erudior-boot and `systemctl status "$(systemd-escape -p --suffix=mount /mnt/erudior-boot)"`. Compare the fstab source with the verified backing file and its signature. Change just erudior-missing.ext4 to erudior-boot.ext4 in the lab row. Reload systemd, verify fstab, and mount that specific entry. Put a file named witness containing `mounted on boot` and a newline on the mounted filesystem. Record its hash and the old boot ID. Reboot a second time. Before manual mount or repair, require a different boot ID, an ext4 mount at that exact mountpoint and the matching witness bytes. Compare an unrelated mount with its baseline. The snapshot provides rollback; this case does not deliberately damage the root filesystem.

Clone after reboot with the deliberately wrong optional mount.

```console
> journalctl -b
Messages for the current boot, including failure to set up the optional mount; q exits the pager.
> findmnt --mountpoint /mnt/erudior-boot
No matching row before the backing path is fixed; a successful mount later produces one ext4 row.
> systemctl status "$(systemd-escape -p --suffix=mount /mnt/erudior-boot)"
Status for the generated mount unit includes the failed mount attempt and its diagnostic.
```

Separately rehearse restoring the course-owned root account using an existing authorized wheel administrator and `sudo passwd root` on a password-enabled test guest. Enter the temporary password interactively. Verify a local console login, compare `id -u` with 0 and restore the documented snapshot afterward. If the normal administrator path is lost, record the required owner authorization, console access, backup and vendor recovery procedure. Never include a password, shadow record or console recording showing one in the handoff.

On the password-enabled disposable guest, use the existing authorized wheel login.

```console
> sudo passwd root
Prompts for the new password and confirmation with input hidden; on success passwd reports the change.
```

Open a separate local guest console and log in as root with the temporary password. In that new session, check the effective user.

```console
> id -u
0
```

lessons.title: Distinguish device presence from driver and configuration
topics: Distinguish device presence from driver and configuration
lessons.body:
An operator says a new data disk vanished. Verify the expected disk's serial, size and bus in the VM configuration first. A filename such as vdb describes enumeration on this boot. Follow the device through the guest rather than forcing a familiar name.

```console
> lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,MODEL,SERIAL,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
A device tree with disk size and any model/serial exposed by the hypervisor.
> lspci -nnk
PCI IDs and kernel driver information for each controller. One controller can serve multiple disks.
> journalctl -k -b
Kernel messages for this boot, including device and driver initialization when logged.
> lsmod
Currently loaded modules with sizes and use counts; built-in drivers can be absent here.
> modinfo virtio_blk
Driver metadata or a local lookup diagnostic if this build supplies no discoverable module information.
```

A PCI controller may present several disks. Built-in drivers do not appear in lsmod as loaded modules and some builds lack a loadable object for the built-in driver. On a virtio guest, compare the controller driver and device links under `/sys/class/block`. If the new virtual disk does not appear in firmware or the hypervisor, changing an fstab UUID cannot make hardware exist.

Practice module parameters with the nonessential **dummy** network driver on a fresh isolated clone. Check `modinfo -p dummy` for `numdummies`. Record whether it is loaded and inspect `ip -br link`. If the module is initially absent, create `/etc/modprobe.d/erudior-dummy.conf` containing `options dummy numdummies=1`, run `sudo modprobe dummy`, then compare `cat /sys/module/dummy/parameters/numdummies` where exported and the observed dummy links. If it was already loaded, changing a file does not reconfigure that live instance. Restore the fresh clone instead of unloading a driver shared with another workload. To schedule the harmless module on the next boot, place the single word `dummy` in `/etc/modules-load.d/erudior-dummy.conf`. Verify after reboot and remove only these exercise files on cleanup.

On the isolated station clone, inspect the parameter and current links before any change.

```console
> modinfo -p dummy
Supported module parameters; look for numdummies.
> ip -br link
One brief row per network link; save the initial names before loading dummy.
> lsmod | awk '$1 == "dummy" {print $1}'
Prints dummy if the loadable module is already loaded. No matching row means it is absent from lsmod.
```

Continue with the load only if the dummy driver was initially absent, the parameter exists and the dedicated modprobe.d file now contains the option shown above. Otherwise restore a fresh clone.

```console
> sudo modprobe dummy
No output on success. The module reads the saved parameter for this fresh load.
> cat /sys/module/dummy/parameters/numdummies
1 if this parameter is exported and the configured value took effect; otherwise compare the resulting links.
```

## Independent practical

On station the work order covers only the course-owned receipt unit, its input and the dummy test module. On separate snapshotted clones the owner also authorizes the lab-only fstab correction, rescue-media identification and recovery of the dedicated clone’s root account. Stage the guided healthy unit; on a snapshot change the service's expected path in a drop-in to a nonexistent name. Hand over the service contract, snapshot, console and module exercise. A separate bootable clone has the deliberately wrong non-root loop-image entry from the console lesson. Identify the faulty layer before editing.

```assignment
lab: startup-practical
```

lessons.title: Read a damaged copy before repairing it
topics: Read a damaged copy before repairing it
lessons.body:
On station create two disposable **regular files** in a new private directory. You will build an ext4 filesystem image containing a known record, duplicate it, and damage only an expendable copy. Keeping the reference bytes outside the image lets you prove data recovery independently of the repair tool's exit status.

```console
> mkdir -m 700 ~/desk-ext-lab
No output when the new private directory is created.
> cd ~/desk-ext-lab
No output on success; subsequent paths resolve here.
> mkdir source
No output; the new source directory exists.
> printf 'north ledger v1\n' > source/ledger
No terminal output; the file contains north ledger v1 and a newline.
> truncate -s 256M origin.img
No output; the regular image has a logical size of 256 MiB.
> mkfs.ext4 -q -F -b 4096 -d source origin.img
The quiet formatter normally prints no output. The disposable image contains an ext4 filesystem populated from source.
> cp --sparse=always origin.img trial.img
No output; trial.img is a separate working copy.
> sha256sum origin.img source/ledger > expected.sha256
No terminal output; the two reference digests are written to expected.sha256.
> dumpe2fs -h origin.img
Filesystem header details including the UUID, block count and 4096-byte block size.
```

Record the backup superblock positions on the clean image with `dumpe2fs origin.img`. In this directory only, write two zero bytes over the ext superblock magic in the expendable image with `printf '\000\000' | dd of=trial.img bs=1 seek=1080 conv=notrunc status=none`. The filesystem starts at byte zero in this particular regular file. Do not transfer these offsets to a disk device. Examine with `e2fsck -fn trial.img`. It may automatically locate a backup, so retain the actual diagnostic and return code. Copy the damaged image to `recover.img` before writing. If the recorded layout has no backup group, use the untouched reference copy as recovery media and explicitly report that method.

Station, in a new private directory.

```console
> dumpe2fs origin.img
The full layout includes group information and any backup superblock locations. Record actual numbers.
```

Damage only trial.img in the fresh private directory. Inspect that copy without writing to it, then duplicate its damaged bytes for recovery.

```console
> printf '\000\000' | dd of=trial.img bs=1 seek=1080 conv=notrunc status=none
No output on success. Only the two specified bytes in trial.img are overwritten.
> e2fsck -fn trial.img
Read-only diagnostic; the primary superblock may be rejected or a backup may be located. Record the actual status.
> cp --sparse=always trial.img recover.img
No output on success. recover.img is a separate copy of the damaged trial.img.
```

If the clean layout listed a backup superblock, enter its actual block number. Repair only recover.img and review any prompts. If the image had no backup group, use the untouched reference as recovery media and document that method.

```console
> read -r -p 'Recorded backup superblock number: ' backup_block
Enter the numeric position from dumpe2fs. The shell saves it without printing a result.
> e2fsck -f -b "$backup_block" -B 4096 recover.img
The checker reports its passes and may ask whether to repair the working copy.
> e2fsck -fn recover.img
The read-only check should finish without unresolved errors after a successful repair.
> debugfs -R 'dump /ledger recovered-ledger' recover.img
debugfs may print its version banner. On success recovered-ledger is created from the filesystem image.
> cmp recovered-ledger source/ledger
No output and exit status 0 when the recovered content matches.
> sha256sum -c expected.sha256
origin.img: OK
source/ledger: OK
```

These checks distinguish a readable superblock, consistent metadata, correct user bytes and preservation of the original. XFS uses different tools. On a separate unmounted XFS working copy, inspect the filesystem in no-modify mode. Review the findings and plan ordinary repair on the copy. Discarding its log can lose committed metadata and requires an explicit recovery decision.

If a separate unmounted XFS fixture is available, supply its actual working-copy path.

```console
> read -r -p 'Unmounted XFS working-copy path: ' xfs_copy
The shell saves the supplied file path.
> xfs_repair -n -f "$xfs_copy"
The read-only check reports its phases and any findings for the regular-file image.
```

lessons.title: Recover access across the LVM layers
topics: Recover access across the LVM layers
lessons.body:
An empty mount does not establish erased data. Determine whether the physical device exists, LVM can read its metadata, the VG is complete, its LV is active, and its filesystem can be mounted. Those checks follow dependencies and narrow the repair.

Use a freshly created regular file in a disposable station guest. As root create `/var/tmp/desk-lvm` as a private directory. In it create a 384 MiB sparse file with `truncate -s 384M pv.img` and attach it using `loop=$(losetup --find --show "$PWD/pv.img")`. Confirm `losetup -j "$PWD/pv.img"` names exactly that loop. If the RHEL-family LVM devices file is in use, use `lvmdevices --adddev "$loop"` for this exercise device as needed. Confirm there is no pre-existing VG called `deskvg` before proceeding. Initialize this **new loop** as a PV and build a lab VG/LV.

As root on the disposable station guest, create a new private directory. If the path already exists, stop and use a fresh snapshot.

```console
> mkdir -m 0700 /var/tmp/desk-lvm
No output on success. The new root-only directory is ready.
> cd /var/tmp/desk-lvm
No output on success. Relative paths now resolve inside the new directory.
```

```console
> truncate -s 384M pv.img
No output; the regular file has a logical size of 384 MiB.
> loop=$(losetup --find --show "$PWD/pv.img")
No terminal output; loop captures the assigned /dev/loopN path.
> losetup -j "$PWD/pv.img"
One record associates the new regular file with the same loop device held in the variable.
```

Only if the devices file is in use and this exercise loop must be added.

```console
> lvmdevices --adddev "$loop"
The verified loop device is registered in the LVM devices file; diagnostic wording depends on version.
```

Before initializing anything, compare the printed loop variable with the one entry for the new backing file. Inspect the existing volume groups and verify that deskvg is absent.

```console
> printf '%s\n' "$loop"
The assigned /dev/loopN device. Its number depends on the guest.
> losetup -j "$PWD/pv.img"
A single row starts with the same loop device and names this exercise image.
> vgs -o vg_name
Lists existing VG names. There must be no deskvg entry for this new exercise.
```

Continue only when the mapping matches, deskvg is unused and /mnt/desk-lvm is an unused exercise mountpoint. These commands initialize the verified new loop and the LV just created on it.

```console
> pvcreate "$loop"
LVM reports creation of the physical volume on your verified loop.
> vgcreate deskvg "$loop"
Volume group "deskvg" successfully created.
> lvcreate -L 96M -n ledger deskvg
Logical volume "ledger" created.
> mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/deskvg/ledger
Normally silent; a new ext4 filesystem is created on the exercise LV.
> mkdir -p /mnt/desk-lvm
No output on success.
> mount /dev/deskvg/ledger /mnt/desk-lvm
No output on success; the LV supplies this mountpoint.
> printf 'ledger 47\n' > /mnt/desk-lvm/receipt
No terminal output; the receipt contains ledger 47 followed by a newline.
> sha256sum /mnt/desk-lvm/receipt
18142a7c2884efe48eb5f26a96ad846dc3a54971592a78e491313068d0cc2823  /mnt/desk-lvm/receipt
> vgcfgbackup -f "$PWD/deskvg.before" deskvg
LVM reports a successful metadata backup and writes deskvg.before.
> umount /mnt/desk-lvm
No output when successfully unmounted.
> lvchange -an deskvg/ledger
On success the LV is inactive.
```

Diagnose from `pvs -o pv_name,pv_uuid,vg_name`, `vgs`, and `lvs -o vg_name,lv_name,lv_attr,devices`. With the PV and VG intact, metadata recreation is unjustified. Activate the existing volume with `lvchange -ay deskvg/ledger`, mount it read-only, and compare the receipt with the saved hash. A `vgcfgbackup` file describes the VG and LVs; it does not contain receipt bytes. For a metadata restoration rehearsal, first map every PV UUID to the course-owned backing files on an offline clone and compare the archive with the proposed VG layout. Use the documented `vgcfgrestore --test -f ... deskvg` as a preview where supported; check the real restore only on an isolated clone. A missing PV calls for locating or restoring that device and its data. Recreating an empty PV with a similar name cannot reconstruct lost extents.

Station root shell after the loop and VG-name checks.

```console
> pvs -o pv_name,pv_uuid,vg_name
The exercise loop retains its PV UUID and belongs to deskvg.
> vgs
A deskvg row reports one PV and the ledger LV.
> lvs -o vg_name,lv_name,lv_attr,devices
The deskvg ledger row still exists; its active flag is absent before recovery.
> lvchange -ay deskvg/ledger
On success the existing LV becomes active; the filesystem can now be mounted read-only.
> mount -o ro /dev/deskvg/ledger /mnt/desk-lvm
No output on success. The recovered LV is mounted read-only.
> sha256sum /mnt/desk-lvm/receipt
18142a7c2884efe48eb5f26a96ad846dc3a54971592a78e491313068d0cc2823  /mnt/desk-lvm/receipt
```

For the optional metadata-restore preview on a separate offline clone, first map every PV UUID back to an exercise backing file and verify the backup matches. Where the installed LVM supports test mode, stay in that clone’s private work directory.

```console
> vgcfgrestore --test -f "$PWD/deskvg.before" deskvg
LVM reports test mode and checks the proposed operation. It does not write the VG metadata.
```

lessons.title: Recover the record with the authorized key
topics: Recover the record with the authorized key
lessons.body:
A locked LUKS container looks like opaque data. Its outer UUID identifies the encrypted container. After unlocking it, the inner filesystem has a different identity. Neither identity grants access. Preserve the key material and header independently of the data.

Use a fresh private directory and an expendable 96 MiB regular file. Make these runs in the disposable VM with a root shell and a saved snapshot. Give the mapper a unique name that is absent from `ls /dev/mapper`. Enter a new exercise-only passphrase at the interactive prompts. Set umask 077 first. Move the resulting header backup to a separate root-only archive after the setup.

Disposable station root shell; compare expected mapper names before the exercise.

```console
> ls /dev/mapper
Lists existing mappings, commonly including control. deskseal must be absent before setup.
> umask 077
No output. Newly created files in this shell default to owner-only access.
```

```console
> truncate -s 96M sealed.img
No output. The fresh regular image is 96 MiB.
> cryptsetup luksFormat --type luks2 sealed.img
The tool warns about initialization and requests confirmation and an exercise passphrase. Input stays hidden.
> cryptsetup luksHeaderBackup sealed.img --header-backup-file desk-header.bak
No output is normal. A sensitive header backup is created; protect it separately.
> cryptsetup luksUUID sealed.img
A LUKS UUID for the outer container. Record the actual value.
> cryptsetup open sealed.img deskseal
Prompts for the authorized exercise passphrase. A successful unlock creates /dev/mapper/deskseal.
> mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/mapper/deskseal
Normally silent; creates ext4 inside the new exercise mapping.
> mkdir -p /mnt/deskseal
No output on success.
> mount /dev/mapper/deskseal /mnt/deskseal
No output on success; the inner ext4 filesystem supplies the mountpoint.
> printf 'signed shift 7\n' > /mnt/deskseal/record
No terminal output; the record is written inside the encrypted fixture.
> sha256sum /mnt/deskseal/record
c31a0945ae5c504605a4f887b34256932d77f3c2a922c2ec8769360840c4e5e8  /mnt/deskseal/record
> umount /mnt/deskseal
No output after a successful unmount.
> cryptsetup close deskseal
No output after a successful close; the mapping disappears.
```

Recover the record on a **copy** of the closed image. Run `cryptsetup isLuks`, inspect `luksDump` without requesting volume-key output, and open the copy with `cryptsetup open --readonly recovery.img deskread` and the known passphrase. Mount the ext4 mapping with `-o ro,noload`, compare the record, unmount and close. If the lab owner supplies a known-good header backup from that exact container, a header restore belongs only on an offline copy with its identity verified first. Valid unlock material remains necessary. If all usable keys are unavailable, preserve the bytes and escalate through the owner's key escrow or data backup. Reformatting destroys the recovery opportunity.

After confirming the mapping is closed, use a new recovery.img in the private directory. Check that deskread is unused and the source is the closed exercise fixture. The header backup belongs in the separate root-only archive.

```console
> cp --sparse=always sealed.img recovery.img
No output on success. recovery.img is a separate copy of the closed container.
> ls /dev/mapper
The existing mapping names are listed. deskread must be absent.
```

Continue on that separate copy with the known exercise key. The filesystem uses an unused exercise mountpoint.

```console
> cryptsetup isLuks recovery.img
No output and status 0 for the copied LUKS container.
> cryptsetup luksDump recovery.img
Header metadata identifies the recorded LUKS UUID and keyslot metadata. No passphrase or volume key is printed.
> cryptsetup open --readonly recovery.img deskread
The authorized passphrase is requested; the opened deskread mapping is read-only.
> mount -o ro,noload /dev/mapper/deskread /mnt/deskseal
No output on success. The inner ext4 filesystem is mounted without journal replay.
> sha256sum /mnt/deskseal/record
c31a0945ae5c504605a4f887b34256932d77f3c2a922c2ec8769360840c4e5e8  /mnt/deskseal/record
> umount /mnt/deskseal
No output on success.
> cryptsetup close deskread
No output on success. The read-only mapping closes.
```

## Independent practical

Use isolated samples, each with a different recorded plaintext hash. Prepare the ext4, loop-backed LVM and sealed LUKS fixtures from the volume lessons on clean snapshots. Stage a damaged primary ext superblock, an inactive healthy LV and a locked copy with an authorized key. A partner retains hashes, the ext layout and the sealed header backup.

```assignment
lab: volumes-practical
```

lessons.title: Distinguish a missing provider from a broken database
topics: Distinguish a missing provider from a broken database
lessons.body:
A package transaction can fail before installation because the configured sources cannot supply a dependency. That problem is separate from an unreadable local RPM database. Use a clean station snapshot with signed, distribution-matched BaseOS and AppStream sources. If using a DVD, both trees must be enabled under the local repository configuration. Keep package signature checking enabled.

Use an authenticated administrative shell on the disposable station guest for the transaction preview.

```console
> dnf repolist --enabled
Enabled repository IDs and names; record the actual local IDs for BaseOS and AppStream.
> dnf list --installed bash
The installed bash package, architecture and version.
> rpm -q --whatprovides /usr/bin/bash
The installed bash package name, version, release and architecture.
> dnf provides '*/semanage'
Matching provider and file information; on the standard EL 10 repository set, look for policycoreutils-python-utils.
> dnf install --assumeno policycoreutils-python-utils
With administrative privilege, expect a proposed transaction followed by an abort, or an already-installed message. No package changes.
```

The first provider query concerns an installed file. DNF can also consult available repository metadata. An aborted transaction following a successful proposal differs from a dependency solver error. If the solver fails, read the precise capability and architecture it requests. Compare it with the packages offered by your enabled repositories. Detect a broken media mount or stale base URL by checking repository information and refreshing metadata only after correcting the source. Installing with dependency checks disabled leaves the original runtime requirement unresolved.

On a never-modified clone, use `dnf --disablerepo='*' --setopt=cachedir=/var/tmp/erudior-empty-cache provides '*/semanage'` as a comparison against the normal enabled sources. Results can include installed ownership if the package is already present, so record initial installation state. The switch applies only to that invocation. Restore normal sources and repeat. Find a matching provider, preview the transaction, then verify the installed binary can perform a read-only help or version request. Save repository IDs and NEVRA rather than a screenshot of a successful progress bar.

Fresh clone, compare this single invocation with the enabled repositories.

```console
> dnf --disablerepo='*' --setopt=cachedir=/var/tmp/erudior-empty-cache provides '*/semanage'
No enabled source can offer a new package; installed matches may still appear. Record what this clone reports.
```

lessons.title: Verify the package record and repair an isolated database copy
topics: Verify the package record and repair an isolated database copy
lessons.body:
An altered file, a dependency failure and a damaged local database need different treatments. RPM verifies installed file attributes against database records; a valid RPM database does not guarantee that a managed configuration is authorized. An approved local edit can be expected drift.

Find the package owning `/etc/issue` with `rpm -qf /etc/issue`. In a fresh disposable guest, save its bytes and metadata with `sudo cp -a /etc/issue /root/desk-issue.before`. Append a lab marker to the installed file. Verify only its owning package using `rpm -Vf /etc/issue`. Read the positions using `man rpm`: a size difference, digest difference and timestamp difference each say something different. Check `rpm -qc PACKAGE` for declared configurations. Save the report before restoring the approved file from the copy, preserving ownership and SELinux labels. Re-run verification and avoid reverting unrelated local changes shown by the same package.

On the disposable station clone, identify the owner and make the archive copy before appending the exercise marker.

```console
> rpm -qf /etc/issue
The name, version, release and architecture of the package owning /etc/issue.
> sudo cp -a /etc/issue /root/desk-issue.before
No output on success; the archive copy preserves the available metadata.
> printf 'erudior issue marker\n' | sudo tee -a /etc/issue >/dev/null
No terminal output. One exercise line is appended to the installed file.
> rpm -Vf /etc/issue
After the marker is appended, the /etc/issue row normally flags changed size, digest and/or modification time.
> man rpm
The local RPM manual opens; q exits the pager.
> rpm -qc "$(rpm -qf /etc/issue)"
Paths registered by the owning package as configuration files.
```

Save the changed-file report. Restore the saved metadata and bytes on this same clone, then compare the new report with the original package state. Other authorized package changes can still appear.

```console
> sudo cp -a /root/desk-issue.before /etc/issue
No output on success. The approved archive copy replaces the exercise edit.
> rpm -Vf /etc/issue
The marker-induced changes to /etc/issue have disappeared. Pre-existing differences can remain.
```

For a database recovery rehearsal, close package managers and confirm no transaction is active on a snapshot clone. Open an authenticated root shell. The SQLite example is for a RHEL-family 10 guest with rpmdb.sqlite. Verify that filename under the path printed by the RPM macro. Run each operation below in that shell. A mode-0700 work directory and an SELinux context copied from the real database allow the confined RPM process to create its temporary rebuild directory **inside this exercise directory**.

```console
> db=$(rpm --eval '%{_dbpath}')
No terminal output; db contains the installed RPM database path.
> work=$(mktemp -d /var/tmp/erudior-rpm.XXXXXXXX)
No terminal output; work contains a newly created private directory.
> chcon --reference="$db" "$work"
No output on success; the directory takes the reference SELinux context.
> mkdir "$work"/{copy,saved,damaged,recovered}
No output; four working subdirectories exist.
> cp -a "$db/." "$work/copy/"
No output; the database contents and metadata are copied.
> chcon -R --reference="$db" "$work"
No output on success; the exercise tree is labeled for the database operations.
> rpmdb --dbpath "$work/copy" --verifydb
A healthy copy normally returns 0 without diagnostics.
> rpm --dbpath "$work/copy" -qa | sort > "$work/before"
No terminal output; before holds the sorted package roster.
> rpmdb --dbpath "$work/copy" --rebuilddb
The copied database is rebuilt; a successful run can be silent.
> rpmdb --dbpath "$work/copy" --verifydb
The rebuilt copy should return 0 without diagnostics.
> rpm --dbpath "$work/copy" -qa | sort > "$work/after"
No terminal output; after holds the rebuilt roster.
> cmp "$work/before" "$work/after"
No output and status 0 when the rosters are identical.
> cp -a "$work/copy/." "$work/saved/"
No output; saved holds the protected matching copy.
> cp -a "$work/copy/." "$work/damaged/"
No output; a separate expendable copy is ready for the drill.
```

Create a fault only in the **damaged copy**. Overwrite its SQLite header with `printf 'BROKENLABHEADER!' | dd of="$work/damaged/rpmdb.sqlite" bs=1 seek=0 conv=notrunc status=none`. Verification of that copy must now fail. Keep the damaged copy for diagnosis. Reconstruct from the matched snapshot using `cp -a "$work/saved/." "$work/recovered/"`. Run verifydb against recovered, regenerate the sorted roster for that path and compare it to before. Finish with `rpm --dbpath "$work/recovered" -qf /usr/bin/bash` and compare with the live ownership query. Structural verification alone does not prove the catalog contains the original packages. A database copied from another guest can be structurally sound and factually wrong.

Authenticated root shell on an idle snapshot clone. All database operations below target its work directory.

```console
> printf 'BROKENLABHEADER!' | dd of="$work/damaged/rpmdb.sqlite" bs=1 seek=0 conv=notrunc status=none
No output; only this damaged copy has its SQLite header overwritten.
> rpmdb --dbpath "$work/damaged" --verifydb
Verification fails with a database read/format diagnostic and a nonzero exit status. The saved copy stays intact.
> cp -a "$work/saved/." "$work/recovered/"
No output; recovered contains the saved database files.
> rpmdb --dbpath "$work/recovered" --verifydb
A healthy recovered copy normally returns status 0 without diagnostics.
> rpm --dbpath "$work/recovered" -qa | sort > "$work/recovered-roster"
No terminal output. The recovered package roster is saved.
> cmp "$work/before" "$work/recovered-roster"
No output and status 0 when the recovered roster matches the original.
> rpm --dbpath "$work/recovered" -qf /usr/bin/bash
The bash package identity should match the same query against this guest’s live database.
> rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash
The package identity should match the ownership query against the recovered copy.
```

## Independent practical

A clean clone has signed source media, one approved reference copy of /etc/issue and a backed-up RPM database copy. Introduce a marker in the package-owned issue file. Use a new, empty cachedir and disable repositories only on one diagnostic invocation. The ticket asks why two different package tools report problems.

```assignment
lab: packaging-practical
```

lessons.title: Work from the client request toward the listener
topics: Work from the client request toward the listener
lessons.body:
The desk report loads on station but fails on relay. A loopback success exercises the application and local TCP stack. It tells you little about the private listener, routing or filtering. Identify the exact protocol, host name, destination port, address family and expected response. In this case the report is HTTP on TCP port 8181.

On station create a new directory `~/desk-web` and put the text `revision=north` followed by a newline in `status`. In one terminal run `python3 -m http.server 8181 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory "$HOME/desk-web"`. In another, request `curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8181/status` and examine `ss -lnt '( sport = :8181 )'`. From relay try the same request using station's private address with a two-second connection timeout. Observe the listener's local address. A firewall change cannot make a loopback-only socket accept private traffic.

Station, terminal A. The status file already contains revision=north and a newline.

```console
> python3 -m http.server 8181 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory "$HOME/desk-web"
The server occupies this terminal until interrupted. Its startup message identifies 127.0.0.1 and port 8181.
```

Station, terminal B, with the foreground server running.

```console
> curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8181/status
revision=north
> ss -lnt '( sport = :8181 )'
A LISTEN row for 127.0.0.1:8181. A loopback-only listener does not accept remote traffic.
```

On relay, enter station’s actual private address and request the loopback-only service.

```console
> read -r -p 'Station private IPv4 address: ' station_ip
The shell stores the supplied private address for this terminal session.
> curl -fsS --connect-timeout 2 "http://$station_ip:8181/status"
The connection fails with a refusal or timeout. The listener only serves station’s loopback address.
```

On station, stop only your foreground server with Ctrl+C. In terminal A enter the actual private address and start the private listener.

```console
> read -r -p 'Station private IPv4 address: ' station_ip
The shell stores the supplied private address for this terminal session.
> python3 -m http.server 8181 --bind "$station_ip" --directory "$HOME/desk-web"
The foreground server announces the private IPv4 address and port 8181. Leave it running.
```

On relay, inspect its chosen route to station.

```console
> ip route get "$station_ip"
A selected interface and source address are shown. A gateway appears when the path needs one. A route alone does not prove a reply.
```

In station’s administrator terminal, identify the zone for its private interface. In that zone permit the test tuple from relay only and check the resulting rule state.

```console
> firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
Active zone names and their bound interfaces or sources. Identify the private interface’s zone.
```

From the same relay shell, verify the expected response over the private network.

```console
> curl -fsS --connect-timeout 2 "http://$station_ip:8181/status"
revision=north
```

If the numeric request succeeds but the name fails, look up the name from relay. Compare with the address that served the record. An optional temporary curl resolver mapping can demonstrate a stale record without modifying host DNS.

```console
> read -r -p 'Station lab hostname: ' station_name
The shell stores the supplied host name.
> getent ahostsv4 "$station_name"
IPv4 records for the supplied name. A lookup failure returns no records and a nonzero status.
```

lessons.title: Use a narrow trace to discriminate between causes
topics: Use a narrow trace to discriminate between causes
lessons.body:
A timeout has several explanations: packets might never leave relay, the wrong server might receive them, a filter might silently drop them, or a reply might use the wrong route. Collect short captures at selected boundaries while one person sends exactly one request.

On station identify the private interface with `ip -br addr`. Open a second terminal on relay. Use this example on station after setting IFACE and CLIENT to the actual lab values. It inspects only the specified test flow.

Station, using the actual interface and relay address on the designated lab flow.

```console
> ip -br addr
Brief device states and addresses; identify the private interface.
```

```console
> sudo timeout 15 tcpdump -nn -i "$IFACE" -c 12 "host $CLIENT and tcp port 8181"
Listening banner, then timestamped packet summaries for the selected flow. Stops at 12 matching packets or 15 seconds; a quiet flow may yield zero packets.
```

While it waits, make the request from relay. A SYN followed by a reset points to an active rejection somewhere on that path. Inspect the local listener and filtering policy before assigning the reset to a particular process. SYN and SYN-ACK without the final ACK shift attention toward the return path or client. A completed handshake followed by HTTP 404 indicates a reachable HTTP endpoint with no matching resource. A capture on the wrong interface can be empty even when the request succeeds. Compare the route-selected interface with the capture interface and record an independent control.

Repeat with the correct port and a deliberately absent path under the same server. Use `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' URL` and compare the successful and failing flows. Retain timestamps, endpoints, flags and HTTP status. Do not capture unrelated payload or authentication traffic. Stop the foreground server and remove only the private rule you introduced after the exercise.

On relay while the bounded capture is running, enter the actual private address. Use the existing report path, then an absent path under the same server. A transport failure can print a diagnostic and a status of 000.

```console
> read -r -p 'Station private IPv4 address: ' station_ip
The shell stores the supplied private address for this terminal session.
> curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$station_ip:8181/status"
200
> curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$station_ip:8181/absent-report"
404
```

## Independent practical

Set up the guided Python server on a fresh station using the new file health with exact bytes south + newline and port 8281. Start it on loopback and limit the private firewall permission to relay. Relay must retrieve the exact bytes over the private IPv4 network. Record one adjacent unused port as the excluded control.

```assignment
lab: network-practical
```

lessons.title: Find the library the loader actually needs
topics: Find the library the loader actually needs
lessons.body:
A binary can exist and still fail before its main function runs. Separate the executable format, dynamic loader, required shared libraries and the application's own input files. Build a tiny application from your own source in a new private working directory. Install the compiler and binutils from your signed lab sources. Save the two files separately.

```c
/* desk.c */
const char *desk(void) { return "north"; }
```

```c
/* main.c */
#include <stdio.h>
extern const char *desk(void);
int main(void) { puts(desk()); return 0; }
```

```console
> gcc -shared -fPIC -Wl,-soname,libdesk.so -o libdesk.so desk.c
No output on a clean compilation; libdesk.so is created.
> gcc -o read-desk main.c -L. -ldesk '-Wl,-rpath,$ORIGIN'
Normally silent. read-desk is linked with a runtime search path relative to itself.
> ./read-desk
north
> readelf -d ./read-desk
Dynamic entries include NEEDED for libdesk.so and a runtime search-path entry containing $ORIGIN.
> mv libdesk.so libdesk.held
No output; the loader’s expected library name is now absent.
> ./read-desk
A loader diagnostic names libdesk.so and says it could not open the shared object. The program exits before printing north.
```

Expect the first run to print north. The second cannot resolve libdesk.so. The NEEDED entry is a library name. The quoted RUNPATH contains a literal loader token resolved relative to the executable. Examine the dynamic section of the **known lab binary** even when the library is absent. Run `strace -e trace=openat -o desk.trace ./read-desk` to observe attempted paths. A failed library lookup elsewhere is normal if a later lookup succeeds. Follow the whole sequence and final error. Restore only the held file and verify the output and exit status. System-wide loader changes would affect unrelated programs.

Within the private build directory with both C files saved.

```console
> strace -e trace=openat -o desk.trace ./read-desk
The loader still reports the missing library on stderr. The attempted openat calls, including failed paths, are written to desk.trace.
```

While the library is still missing, keep desk.trace as evidence. Restore the held library in this build directory and retest the same executable.

```console
> mv libdesk.held libdesk.so
No output on success. The library is back under its required name.
> ./read-desk
north
> printf '%s\n' "$?"
0
```

lessons.title: Test a growth hypothesis under fixed input
topics: Test a growth hypothesis under fixed input
lessons.body:
The RSS of a worker rose while requests were served. An allocator can retain previously used pages, a cache can warm up, and a queue can grow when producers outpace consumers. A leak hypothesis needs repeated equivalent work and a comparison when work drains. Save this bounded teaching fixture as `worker.py` in a fresh directory.

```python
import sys
import time
history = []
for batch in range(12):
    item = bytearray(1024 * 1024)
    if sys.argv[1] == "retain":
        history.append(item)
    print(batch, len(history), flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.5)
time.sleep(2)
```

Launch `python3 worker.py retain > retain.log &`, save `pid=$!` immediately in that shell, and sample `ps -p "$pid" -o pid,etime,rss,vsz,comm` once per second until the worker exits. Repeat with `release` under the same environment. RSS is resident memory; VSZ includes address space that may have no resident pages. The program deliberately retains reachable objects. That explains this fixture's trend without establishing an unreachable C allocation or a kernel leak. Save the sample stream and application record. If memory stops growing in the release run, identify which retained reference changed and which workload remained equivalent.

On station, same shell, with worker.py saved in the private directory.

```console
> python3 worker.py retain > retain.log &
In interactive Bash, a job number and PID may appear; the worker’s batch records go to retain.log.
> pid=$!
No output. pid holds the background worker’s PID.
> ps -p "$pid" -o pid,etime,rss,vsz,comm
A header and a row for the running Python process. RSS and VSZ are reported in KiB; later samples vary.
```

Sample once per second until the retain worker ends, then repeat the same workload without retaining prior batches. Save the samples with their elapsed times. The final log record reports the zero-based batch number and retained object count.

```console
> tail -n 1 retain.log
11 12
> python3 worker.py release > release.log &
In interactive Bash a job number and PID may appear. Records go to release.log.
> pid=$!
No output. The variable now holds the release worker’s PID.
> ps -p "$pid" -o pid,etime,rss,vsz,comm
A header and a row for the running release worker. Compare RSS at equivalent sampling times.
```

After sampling the release worker through completion, check its last record.

```console
> tail -n 1 release.log
11 0
```

Review the course's MIT profiling reference and use `journalctl -k -b` to look for actual kernel memory-pressure evidence if a real service was killed. Compare cgroup `memory.events` counters around a controlled test. A missing process plus an empty global kernel log is insufficient to infer a leak. A production-quality report states sample duration, workload, per-process trend, cgroup scope and uncertainty.

On station, same shell, with worker.py saved in the private directory.

```console
> journalctl -k -b
Kernel records for the current boot; look for actual memory-pressure events before attributing a process exit to them.
```

lessons.title: Restore a service's intended SELinux access
topics: Restore a service's intended SELinux access
lessons.body:
A file can be world-readable and still be inaccessible to a confined service. Traditional permissions govern traversal and reads; SELinux independently evaluates a process domain, object label and requested operation. Compare the failing service's actual path with a known working control before changing policy.

Use a private disposable guest with enforcing SELinux, Apache, audit tools and semanage installed. First run Apache with its default document root and verify a unique local marker across HTTP. Back up any existing lab configuration. Create a new tree `/srv/erudior-public` with traversable directories, a readable index.html and a dedicated Apache configuration alias `/desk/` pointing there. Include a matching Directory block with `Require all granted`. Validate the Apache configuration, reload it and request `http://127.0.0.1/desk/index.html`. A failure is meaningful only after confirming the listener, route, alias and Unix permissions. Compare `ls -Zd` for the new tree with the standard document root, `ps -eZ` for the service, and `sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent` for a denial corresponding to the request.

Station, after verifying the default site and setting up the lab alias.

```console
> ls -Zd /srv/erudior-public /var/www/html
Both directories’ SELinux contexts and paths. Compare their type fields.
> ps -eZ
Process labels and names; look for httpd processes and their security domain.
> sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent
Recent matching audit records or a no-matches result. Correlate timestamp, path and domain with the failed request.
```

When the observed denial names the shared file and the intended policy is ordinary read-only web content, add the persistent mapping with `sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/erudior-public(/.*)?'` if that lab mapping is absent. Apply it using `sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/erudior-public`. If a matching local mapping already exists, inspect it before deciding whether to modify it. Retest exact HTTP bytes as a client, confirm enforcing mode, run restorecon again, then retest. If the objects already have an allowed type and no relevant denial appears, investigate Apache and filesystem permissions. Generating a broad allow rule obscures that distinction.

Station, only when evidence shows the missing mapping and an equivalent local rule does not already exist.

```console
> sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/erudior-public(/.*)?'
No output on successful addition. The persistent mapping has been recorded.
> sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/erudior-public
Changed paths are reported with their labels. A second run on already-correct labels can be silent.
```

lessons.title: Separate identity lookup from account eligibility
topics: Separate identity lookup from account eligibility
lessons.body:
A user's name resolves and their public key has the correct permissions, yet their scheduled login is rejected. Identity resolution tells you that a record exists. Authentication establishes identity. Account management can still refuse admission because of a policy such as expiration. Session setup can fail even after admission.

As root on a clone with an authenticated administrator console, create the disposable user `desklearner` if absent. Set an interactive lab-only password using `passwd desklearner`. Record `getent passwd desklearner`, `id desklearner`, `passwd -S desklearner`, and `chage -l desklearner`. Do not collect password hashes. Confirm a successful local console login as that user. Save a second administrator shell and keep it open throughout.

Station, authorized root console on a snapshot clone with desklearner present.

```console
> passwd desklearner
The password tool prompts twice without echoing input and confirms a successful change.
> getent passwd desklearner
A colon-separated account record starts with desklearner: and includes its assigned UID, home and shell.
> id desklearner
UID, GID and groups for the dedicated account. Numeric values vary.
> passwd -S desklearner
One password-status record, with the status and aging fields for desklearner; it does not print a password hash.
> chage -l desklearner
Labeled password-aging and account-expiration values. Preserve the separate fields.
```

Set an **account expiration date** in the past using `chage -E 2001-01-01 desklearner`. Try the same console login again, capture the local journal at the observed time, and compare account expiration with the separate password-aging fields. An account with a current password can be expired. Repair only the exercise account with `chage -E -1 desklearner` if the work order calls for no expiration, then verify by performing the login again. Express site policy explicitly; setting account expiry to never is appropriate here solely because this lab account's baseline says so.

Keep the authenticated administrator console open. Confirm a successful login as desklearner on a second console, then log that test session out. In the administrator console, expire only the exercise account.

```console
> chage -E 2001-01-01 desklearner
No output on success. The lab account’s expiration date is set in the past.
```

Attempt the same desklearner login again on the second console. Record the refusal and its time. From the held administrator console, compare the expiration date with the password-aging fields and collect the local journal entries for that attempt.

```console
> chage -l desklearner
The account-expiration field shows 2001-01-01 in the local date format. The password-aging fields are separate.
> journalctl -b --since '5 minutes ago'
Current-boot journal entries from the recent interval. Match the login attempt by time and preserve the specific account-admission evidence.
```

After preserving the result, restore the exercise baseline from the administrator console.

```console
> chage -E -1 desklearner
No output on success. Account expiration is removed, matching this specific exercise baseline.
> chage -l desklearner
The account-expiration field shows never on an English-language guest.
```

Repeat the same desklearner login on the second console. It should succeed when all other account and session checks pass.

Compare this with a recorded lockout counter on a guest whose authselect profile enables faillock. Inspect `authselect current`, `authselect check`, `faillock --user desklearner` and the local faillock policy. An empty counter alone does not prove a login should succeed. Clear only the named learner's counter after resolving its cause and confirming authorization. Keep the test of an excluded account separate from the repaired positive case.

Station, authorized root console on a snapshot clone with desklearner present.

```console
> authselect current
The selected authentication profile and enabled features on an authselect-managed guest.
> authselect check
A valid managed configuration is reported when the current files match.
> faillock --user desklearner
That user’s recent failed-authentication entries if any are recorded, or no records. Account expiration is independent.
```

lessons.title: Repair a dedicated PAM policy stack
topics: Repair a dedicated PAM policy stack
lessons.body:
Each PAM-aware program supplies a service name that selects a stack. The account rules for a custom desk application can deny a person whose normal shell login succeeds. A rule marked required records failure even if a later required module succeeds. Work with a **new service named erudior-desk**. Leave the profiles serving SSH, sudo and the console alone.

In the disposable station guest create `desklearner` and `deskvisitor` as local lab-only users. As root create `/etc/erudior-admit` containing the single line `desklearner`, owned by root with mode 0644. Save this stack as `/etc/pam.d/erudior-desk` and restore its default SELinux context. The list file is an authorization allowlist, with a closed-on-error behavior.

```text
account required pam_listfile.so item=user sense=allow file=/etc/erudior-admit onerr=fail
account required pam_unix.so
```

Use the small **PAM account probe** in References to run account checks for both users. It uses the actual PAM library, asks only whether the named account may use this service and never requests credentials. The allowed user should pass and the visitor should fail. Change only the list-file path in the dedicated service to point to an absent file. Test again. Reading the control rule, checking the expected file and comparing the unchanged account status localizes the failure.

Restore the intended file path. Verify both the accepted person and the excluded visitor. A blanket pam_permit change could make the positive test pass while exposing the service to everyone. Check `authselect check` separately on a system managed by authselect. Lasting site-wide changes belong in supported features or an appropriately managed custom profile; editing generated system-auth files by hand creates drift. Keep the service's private test harness and admission observations in the case record.

On a guest managed by authselect.

```console
> authselect check
Reports whether the selected profile’s managed configuration is valid.
```

lessons.title: Prepare a crash capture and validate the result
topics: Prepare a crash capture and validate the result
lessons.body:
A regular journal ends at the crash. Kdump reserves memory for a second kernel that can boot after the primary kernel fails and write the first kernel's memory to a configured destination. A listening service, a reserved region, a loaded crash kernel and an actual dump are four different observations.

Use a separate disposable guest with console access, adequate RAM, free dump storage and a restorable snapshot. Install kexec-tools. Review `/etc/kdump.conf` with `man kdump.conf`. Identify the destination filesystem, intended path and free space. Paths are interpreted relative to the configured dump target. Inspect the following as administrator.

Separate dump guest, administrator shell.

```console
> man kdump.conf
The local manual opens. Check target and path semantics, and use q to exit.
```

```console
> cat /proc/cmdline
Arguments for the running kernel; record any crashkernel reservation parameter.
> cat /sys/kernel/kexec_crash_size
Reserved crash-kernel size in bytes. A positive number shows reserved memory; 0 means none.
> cat /sys/kernel/kexec_crash_loaded
1 when a crash kernel is loaded, 0 otherwise.
> kdumpctl status
Operational or non-operational diagnostic for the installed kdump service and environment.
> systemctl status kdump
The kdump unit’s load/active state and recent service messages.
> df -h /var/crash
Capacity and available space on the filesystem containing /var/crash; compare with the actual configured dump target.
```

If the guest has no reservation, consult the matching RHEL 10 kernel guide for its architecture and RAM. On supported builds `kdumpctl reset-crashkernel --kernel=ALL` applies the distribution's defaults to boot entries. Save the original entries first, reboot the clone under supervision, and verify the running command line and reserved bytes. Enable and start kdump, inspect its journal and check that the crash kernel is loaded. A read-only or full destination remains a risk even with a loaded kernel.

Only on supported builds with a missing reservation, saved boot entries and supervision.

```console
> kdumpctl reset-crashkernel --kernel=ALL
The distribution defaults are applied to the selected boot entries. Verify the running reservation only after reboot.
```

For the hands-on capture, use the guide's documented **test kdump configuration** procedure on the designated throwaway VM, with its owner observing the console, no other workload and a saved snapshot. The test intentionally reboots the primary system. After recovery locate the newly timestamped vmcore and accompanying kernel messages, record sizes and restricted ownership, and correlate the new boot ID with the test time. A stale dump does not pass. If the platform cannot perform a controlled crash, complete readiness and analyze an instructor-supplied sanitized dump; record the live-capture outcome as unverified. Memory dumps may contain credentials and user data. Keep them on the protected lab guest.

lessons.title: Select, redact and verify a support bundle
topics: Select, redact and verify a support bundle
lessons.body:
A support engineer needs the reproduction time, symptom, affected release, failing subsystem and comparison that rules out a competing explanation. A large attachment without these facts may be less useful than a short, precise timeline. A digest identifies the bytes collected, not the truth of their contents.

Make a new root-only case directory. Record the affected guest's UTC time, boot ID and OS/kernel releases. Reproduce one harmless failed unit on the clone and save only its relevant journal interval. Run `sudo sos report --batch --clean` after inspecting the installed tool's help. The command reports an archive path under a temporary directory. Capture the exact path and exit status; never select a bundle by guessing which file is newest when several people are working. Redaction changes what an engineer can correlate, so preserve a separate protected original only if local policy requires one.

On the designated guest, authorized administrator, locally only.

```console
> sudo sos report --batch --clean
Plugin and cleaning progress are followed by the generated archive path and related evidence. Record the actual path and exit status.
```

As root inspect the archive's member listing with `tar -tf ARCHIVE`, note the sections relevant to your incident and inspect a narrow sample locally. Check for private addresses, hostnames, tokens, usernames, custom logs and command lines with sensitive arguments before any transfer. Compute `sha256sum ARCHIVE` and archive size. Tie it to a short timeline with the observed result, expected result, actions taken, unsuccessful hypotheses and rollback state. Generate and review only; transfer is outside this exercise.

In the local administrator shell, enter the exact archive path that sos reported. Review the member listing and a narrow local sample before any transfer.

```console
> read -r -p 'Exact sos archive path: ' archive
The shell stores the supplied path.
> tar -tf "$archive"
Member paths from this specific support archive.
> sha256sum "$archive"
A 64-character hexadecimal digest and the exact archive path.
> stat -c %s "$archive"
The size of this archive in bytes.
```

A crash dump and a support archive are complementary. Kdump captures a point-in-time memory image after a crash. Sos collects a broad set of current configuration and diagnostics from its running environment. When a host no longer boots, indiscriminately running sos in installer rescue can describe the rescue environment. Identify the source of every file and annotate any evidence copied from the installed root.

## Independent practical

Use a separate dump-capable disposable guest and a sanitized course incident. Stage a new failing unit and reproduce once, then provision and test a local crash capture through the documented supervised vendor procedure. Generate the support bundle after recovery. An instructor-supplied capture allows interpretation practice if the guest cannot test kdump; mark capture unverified and score it separately.

```assignment
lab: support-practical
```

lessons.title: Restore the east desk and produce a defensible handoff
topics: Restore the east desk and produce a defensible handoff
lessons.body:
Start on fresh station and relay snapshots. Read **Case setup for instructors** for the independent exercise preparation and ask the lab partner to prepare the east desk. Solo learners may stage the named fixtures, close the setup guide and treat the affected layers as known. Evidence from worked examples earns no marks here. Capture the starting boot IDs and a reference hash stored away from station.

Relay's user needs the exact file `/ticket` at the specified private address and TCP port 8282. It must contain the bytes `east ticket 19` followed by a newline. The operating system must reach its normal target, the desk service must start automatically, and requests to an unrelated port must retain their original behavior. A separate ext4 image holds the audit receipt. Recover it on a copy and deliver the exact expected receipt without writing the original image. A fresh marker must reach the relay log if the lab has configured centralized logging in the observation practical.

1. Establish two independent observations before changing anything. Compare unit and input state, listener tuple, client path, and the image's expected metadata. Record a plausible explanation that the next test can distinguish.
2. Restore the minimum configuration and data required by the work order. Record the effective service configuration, numeric endpoint, expected receipt hash and a test of the excluded port. Explain why recreating the filesystem or relaxing a global policy would be excessive.
3. Reboot station and verify the new boot ID, exact remote bytes and enabled service **before** restarting any service or rerunning configuration management. Compare the original image hash to the preincident record. Confirm postboot behavior of the excluded port against its baseline.
4. Prepare a timeline and local redacted evidence index for the incoming administrator. Name the remaining uncertainty, one rollback point and how another person can reproduce the application request and the recovered-byte check.

Use the assignment named **East desk final** in Assignments to submit the record. Its four criteria are scored independently. Log delivery earns evidence only when both ends were configured and the receiver shows this run's unique marker. A skipped environment-dependent activity must be identified in the submission.

cards.topic: Build a record another shift can reproduce
cards.front: What does load average count besides runnable work?
cards.back: Tasks in uninterruptible sleep can also contribute. Inspect CPU idle and blocked work before inferring CPU contention.

cards.front: When a Cockpit history graph is blank, what should you record?
cards.back: The selected guest and interval, collector availability and live observations. Missing history is not a zero measurement.

cards.front: How do you validate an rsyslog configuration before restarting it?
cards.back: Run rsyslogd -N1 on the machine that will load the configuration.

cards.topic: Follow one message from producer to collector
cards.front: What failure can an in-memory queue conceal temporarily?
cards.back: Temporary loss of the receiver. Restarting the sender may lose buffered messages.

cards.topic: Separate approved changes from unexplained drift
cards.front: Why check both a hash and a mode?
cards.back: Identical bytes can have the wrong access policy; the correct mode can protect incorrect bytes.

cards.back: The limit and verified inventory constrain which hosts can change and support a meaningful excluded-host check.

cards.front: Why can a login prompt coexist with a failed wanted unit?
cards.back: The target can complete despite failure of a wanted service. Inspect the unit and the exact customer operation.

cards.topic: Read the failed dependency before changing the service
cards.front: What does active (exited) mean for this exercise's oneshot service?
cards.back: Its successful process exited and RemainAfterExit retains active state. Read the receipt separately.

cards.front: Why might journalctl --list-boots show only one boot?
cards.back: Previous journals might have been volatile or rotated away. Record the evidence actually available.

cards.back: Identify installed root versus rescue root, the confirmed storage identity, changed files and successful installed-system boot.

cards.front: Does missing output in lsmod alone rule out a driver?
cards.back: No. A driver can be built into the kernel. Compare sysfs links and device binding.

cards.topic: Distinguish device presence from driver and configuration
cards.front: Why record disk serial and bus as well as name?
cards.back: The enumeration name can change. Independent identifiers help select the intended device.

cards.front: Which tools provide read-only inspection for ext4 and XFS respectively?
cards.back: e2fsck -fn on the unmounted ext4 copy, and xfs_repair -n on an unmounted XFS copy.

cards.topic: Read a damaged copy before repairing it

cards.back: The recorded original bytes are unchanged. The recovered member still needs its own check.

cards.front: Why does an empty mount directory reveal little about underlying data?
cards.back: It might be the bare mountpoint. Inspect findmnt and LV activation before concluding that files were lost.
